content.title: What is ibogaine, the psychedelic drug Trump approved for research?
content.text: The root-bark extract has been cited as a game-changer for those with PTSD or addiction — but the risks appear to be high Conor McGregor, who met President Trump in the Oval Office last year, said an ibogaine treatment “saved his life”X Saturday April 18 2026, 3.56pm BST, The Times President Trump has signed an executive order that encourages more scientific research into a psychedelic drug used to treat post-traumatic stress disorder and addiction. Ibogaine is a naturally occurring psychoactive compound extracted from the root bark of the west African shrub Tabernanthe iboga. Ibogaine affects opioid receptors, which are involved in pain and addiction, but it does so differently than drugs such as heroin or methadone. It influences dopamine pathways related to reward and motivation, as well as NMDA receptors, which are linked to learning. US newsletter A balanced, fair and fact-checked take on global news and culture for our US readers. People who undergo ibogaine treatment often report a significant reduction in withdrawal symptoms and cravings. Patients usually take it by swallowing the powder mixed with water, overseen by a trained practitioner who calculates the dose based on weight and tolerance. A treatment at a clinic in Mexico The experience is typically long and intense, lasting anywhere from 12 to 36 hours, and often includes vivid visions, memories and a kind of “life review”. It is usually overseen by the practitioner in a safe environment. Conor McGregor, the Irish mixed martial arts fighter, revealed last year that he underwent an intense 36-hour ibogaine treatment in Tijuana, Mexico, to address “past trauma”, describing the experience as life-changing. He claimed the psychedelic therapy allowed him to “see his own death” and resulted in a profound spiritual experience that he says “saved his life”. Inside the Mexican ibogaine clinic where Conor McGregor ‘saw Jesus’ The podcaster Joe Rogan joined the president in the Oval Office as he signed the executive order, despite a number of critical comments he has made, aimed at Trump’s handling of the Iran war. Rogan said he texted the president requesting fast-tracked research. “The text message came back [from Trump]: ‘Sounds great! Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it!’” Rogan told reporters. The drug has a schedule-one classification in the US, the same as heroin Some studies indicate that ibogaine can successfully reduce PTSD, depression, addiction and other disorders, but there are serious health risks. A 2023 report reviewing two dozen studies involving more than 700 people documented at least 27 deaths after ibogaine use. One of the most significant concerns is its effect on the heart, as it can cause irregular heart rhythms that may be fatal. The executive order directs the Food and Drug Adminstration (FDA) to “facilitate and establish a pathway for eligible patients to access psychedelic drugs, including ibogaine compounds”. The Department of Health will also allocate at least $50 million to “develop programs to advance psychedelic drugs for serious mental illnesses.” Ibogaine presently holds a schedule-one classification in the US, alongside drugs including heroin and ecstasy. This legal status forces many Americans, including veterans suffering from PTSD, to travel to Mexico and other countries to access clinics offering the drug. Unsanctioned use of the drug spread in the United States after 1962, when an American named Howard Lotsof tried ibogaine and found that it cured him of his addiction to heroin. Howard Lotsof Nonprofit groups have in recent years assisted military veterans in using ibogaine to treat combat-related traumas, which has led to support from political leaders, including Republicans — who are rarely supportive of psychedelics. This smart new shroom chocolate is magic (and legal) Several states with considerable veteran populations have invested in ibogaine-research initiatives. Texas approved $50 million for research last year while Oklahoma, Mississippi and Arizona have expanded state-level research programmes. Kyrsten Sinema, a former Democratic and independent US senator for Arizona, pushed for funds to be dedicated to clinical ibogaine trials to treat veterans after learning about its ibogaine treatments from military personnel she knew and trying it herself. California advanced psychedelic drug research in 2025 when its governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1103, legislation designed to accelerate and streamline the approval process for psychedelic-drug research.
